rules.name: Five Vowel System
rules.description: Dimasa maintains a core five-vowel system consisting of /i, e, a, o, u/ without phonemic vowel length contrast in native roots.
rules.explanation: Native Dimasa roots exhibit five tense vowel phonemes. Lax vowel variants emerge phonetically in unstressed or epenthetic positions.

rules.name: 17 Consonant Phoneme Inventory
rules.description: Dimasa has 17 native consonant phonemes with a two-way stop voicing contrast: /p, b, t, d, k, g, ʔ, m, n, ŋ, ɾ, s, z, h, w, l, j/.
rules.formula: C -> { p, b, t, d, k, g, ʔ, m, n, ŋ, ɾ, s, z, h, w, l, j }
rules.explanation: Voiced aspirates and retroflex stops only appear in unassimilated Indo-Aryan loanwords and are not part of native Dimasa phonology.

rules.name: Sesquisyllabic Word Structure
rules.description: Initial consonant clusters phonetically surface with a weak epenthetic schwa-like transitional vowel, creating a 1.5 syllable structure.
rules.explanation: Underlying clusters with prefix g- or initial stops are realized with a minor unstressed pre-syllable, typical of conservative Bodo-Garo phonetics.

rules.name: Glottal Stop and Velar Nasal Distribution
rules.description: The glottal stop /ʔ/ and velar nasal /ŋ/ are phonotactically prohibited in word-initial position in native Dimasa vocabulary.
rules.explanation: Velar nasal /ŋ/ occurs exclusively in syllable-coda and medial intervocalic positions.

rules.name: Roman Orthography Standardization
rules.description: Standard Dimasa orthography approved by the Dimasa Sahitya Sabha employs the Latin alphabet with digraphs 'kh', 'ph', 'th', 'sh', and 'ng'.
rules.formula: Graphemes: a, b, d, e, g, h, i, j, k, l, m, n, o, p, r, s, t, u, w, y; digraphs: kh, ph, th, ng
rules.explanation: Standard orthographic conventions adopted by the Dimasa Sahitya Sabha for academic and public documentation.

rules.name: Bengali-Assamese Script Representation
rules.description: In regional literature and historical texts, Dimasa has been written using the Eastern Nagari (Bengali/Assamese) script.
rules.formula: Roman <-> Eastern Nagari: di <-> দি, noh <-> নহ, grao <-> গ্রাও
rules.explanation: Bengali/Assamese characters represent Dimasa phonemes historically in Cachar and earlier Assam publications.

rules.name: Nominal Compounding (Root + Root)
rules.description: Nouns are formed by concatenating monosyllabic lexical roots, with head-initial or modifier-head compounding.
rules.explanation: Extremely productive morphological mechanism in Bodo-Garo languages.

rules.name: Human Plural Suffix -rao
rules.description: Human and animate nouns mark plural number using the collective plural suffix -rao.
rules.explanation: Inanimate nouns usually do not take -rao and instead rely on context, numeral classifiers, or quantifiers like gbang-ba (many).

rules.name: Personal Pronoun System
rules.description: Personal pronouns distinguish 1st, 2nd, and 3rd person in singular and plural, exhibiting first-person suppletive plural stems.
rules.formula: 1SG: ang, 1PL: ching; 2SG: ning, 2PL: nisi; 3SG: bo, 3PL: bosi
rules.explanation: First person plural shows suppletive stem change from ang to ching, a foundational Bodo-Garo typological trait.

rules.name: Velar Nasal Deletion Before Coronal Case Suffixes
rules.description: First and second person pronoun stems ending in -ng delete the final velar nasal when attaching the genitive suffix -ni or dative -ne.
rules.formula: ang + -ni -> ani; ning + -ni -> nini; ching + -ni -> chini
rules.explanation: Morphophonemic rule: -ng -> ∅ / __ + n. The final velar nasal drops completely before alveolar nasal initial suffixes.

rules.name: Nominative / Absolutive Zero Marking
rules.description: The nominative case for clausal subjects of transitive and intransitive verbs is unmarked (zero morpheme).
rules.explanation: Subject arguments in neutral citation and clause positions carry no overt suffix.

rules.name: Accusative Differential Object Marking -ke / -khe
rules.description: Definite and specific direct objects are marked by the accusative clitic -ke or -khe.
rules.explanation: Indefinite or non-specific objects typically lack overt accusative marking.

rules.name: Genitive Possession Marker -ni
rules.description: Possessive relationships and noun modification are marked by the genitive suffix -ni on the possessor noun phrase.
rules.explanation: Head-final genitive construction where possessor precedes the possessed head noun.

rules.name: Dative / Benefactive Marker -ne / -thane
rules.description: Indirect objects, recipients, and beneficiaries are marked by -ne or the expanded form -thane.
rules.explanation: Pronominal stems assimilate before -thane: ang + thane -> anthane; ning + thane -> ninthane.

rules.name: Locative Case Marker -ha
rules.description: Spatial location, position, and static presence ('at, in, on') are marked by the locative postposition -ha.

examples.translation: There are fish in the water

rules.explanation: Attaches directly to noun phrases or place names to signify static spatial location or directional endpoint.

rules.name: Ablative Source Marker -niphang / -nipra
rules.description: Movement away from a location or source ('from') is marked by the compound ablative suffix -niphang or -nipra.
rules.explanation: A composite postposition combining genitive -ni with directional base -phang / -pra.

rules.name: Instrumental Marker -shi / -neha
rules.description: The instrument or means by which an action is performed is indicated by -shi or -neha.
rules.explanation: Identifies instrumental agency in transitive clauses.

rules.name: Comitative / Sociative Marker -ba / -jawa
rules.description: Comitative association ('with, along with') is marked by postpositions -ba, -jawa, or -lai.
rules.explanation: Expresses accompaniment and additive discourse relation.

rules.name: Neutrality of Person and Gender Agreement
rules.description: Dimasa verbs do not inflect for grammatical person (1st, 2nd, 3rd) or gender; the verb form is determined strictly by TAM and polarity.
rules.explanation: Unlike Indo-Aryan languages, Dimasa predicates have zero agreement morphology for person or gender.

rules.name: Present Imperfective / Continuous -du
rules.description: The suffix -du marks present imperfective, progressive, and ongoing actions in the present time.
rules.explanation: Standard marker of present ongoing action or current stative event.

rules.name: Non-Future Imperfective / Past -ba
rules.description: The suffix -ba marks non-future imperfective and narrative past events.
rules.explanation: Primary past narrative tense-aspect marker in Dimasa discourse.

rules.name: Past Perfective / Completive -kadu
rules.description: Completed actions with persisting present relevance are marked by the completive aspect suffix -kadu.
rules.explanation: Marks aspectual completion prior to reference time.

rules.name: Future / Prospective Tense -ma / -nang
rules.description: Future intentions, predictions, and upcoming events are marked by the prospective suffix -ma or -nang.
rules.explanation: The marker -ma is the standard future tense marker across Dimasa dialects.

rules.name: Imperative Suffix -bo
rules.description: Affirmative imperative directives and requests are formed by suffixing -bo to the bare verb root.
rules.explanation: Standard affirmative command or polite request form.

rules.name: Prohibitive Prefix da- (Negative Imperative)
rules.description: Negative commands ('don't do X!') are formed by prefixing da- to the verb stem without the imperative suffix.
rules.explanation: The prohibitive prefix da- attaches directly to the verb stem and blocks affirmative imperative marking.

rules.name: General Negative Suffix -ja / -ya
rules.description: Declarative negation is formed by suffixing -ja or -ya to the verb stem.

examples.translation: I do not go / I will not go

rules.explanation: Standard polarity negation marker attaching directly to verbal roots.

rules.name: Tense-Aspect Neutralization Under Negation
rules.description: In negated verbal clauses, fine-grained tense-aspect distinctions (such as -du or -ba) are collapsed and omitted in favor of the bare negative suffix -ja.

examples.translation: He is going -> He is not going
I saw -> I did not see

rules.explanation: Crucial typological feature of Dimasa documented by Evans & Langthasa (2024): polarity overrides aspectual suffixation slots.

rules.name: Suppletive Negative Existential Copula giri
rules.description: Absence and non-existence are expressed through the dedicated negative copula giri, which suppletes the affirmative existential dong.

examples.translation: There is water in the house
There is no water in the house

rules.explanation: Negative copula giri functions as an independent lexical predicate indicating non-existence or absence.

rules.name: SOV Basic Word Order
rules.description: Dimasa is canonically head-final with canonical Subject - Object - Verb clause order.
rules.explanation: Verb always occupies the clause-final predicate position in neutral declarative clauses.

rules.name: Head-Final Postpositional Phrasing
rules.description: Dimasa utilizes postpositions rather than prepositions; relational markers follow the noun phrase.
rules.explanation: Direct correlate of canonical OV clausal typology.

rules.name: Polar Interrogative Particle -na
rules.description: Yes/no questions are formed by appending the interrogative enclitic -na to the clause-final predicate.
rules.explanation: Cliticizes to the final verb to convert declarative clauses into polar questions.

rules.name: In-Situ Content Questions (Wh-in-situ)
rules.description: Wh-interrogative words (sar, tamah, baha, baphai, bedehe, nadinang) remain in-situ in their canonical syntactic argument positions.
rules.explanation: Question words do not front to clause-initial position unlike in English.

rules.name: Numeral Classifier Syntax and Definiteness Correlation
rules.description: Dimasa requires numeral classifiers when counting nouns. Word order correlates with definiteness: Classifier-Numeral + Noun is indefinite, Noun + Classifier-Numeral is definite.
rules.explanation: Prominent typological feature in Dimasa syntax documented by Longmailai (2014) and Evans & Langthasa (2024).

rules.name: Human Classifier sao-
rules.description: Human beings are counted using the numeral classifier sao- (derived from the lexical root for 'body').
rules.explanation: Obligatory classifier for all human referents.

rules.name: Rigid Long Object Classifier gong-
rules.description: Long, rigid, cylindrical, and stick-like objects (pens, sticks, horns, weapons) are classified by gong- / gon-.
rules.explanation: Classifies objects according to long, rigid 1D dimensional shape.

rules.name: Tree and Plant Classifier phang-
rules.description: Trees, plants, bushes, and growing woody stalks are counted using the classifier phang-.
rules.explanation: Semantic classifier specialized for botanical flora.

rules.name: Flat Object Classifier khang-
rules.description: Flat, 2-dimensional sheet-like items (paper, leaves, mats) take the classifier khang-.
rules.explanation: Classifies objects according to planar 2D dimensional shape.

rules.name: Default and Animate Classifier ma-
rules.description: Animals, non-human living beings, and generic counting objects take the default classifier ma-.
rules.explanation: Serves both as the generic default classifier and as the specialized animal classifier.

rules.name: Adjectival Prefixation with g- / ge-
rules.description: Descriptive adjectives are derived from stative roots by prefixing g- / ge- / gd-.
rules.explanation: Shared archaic Bodo-Garo morphological prefix marking nominalized attributes.

rules.name: Complete Verbal Reduplication for Intensification
rules.description: Verbal and adjectival stems undergo full reduplication to indicate iterative action, continuous state, or intensification.
rules.explanation: Productive iconicity strategy in Dimasa oral discourse.
